questions.question_text:
A department's $6$ staff have a mean weekly wage of $\$540$ and population standard deviation $\$61$.
Every staff member receives a $\$45$ pay rise.
What are the new mean and standard deviation?

options.text: $\overline{x} = \$585, \ \sigma_x = \$106$
options.why: Applied the $\$45$ rise to the mean and also added it to the standard deviation, treating $\sigma_x$ as if it shifted with the data.

options.text: $\overline{x} = \$585, \ \sigma_x = \$61$
$\overline{x} = \$540, \ \sigma_x = \$61$
options.why: Decided a pay rise changes nothing at all, so neither the mean nor the standard deviation was updated.

options.text: $\overline{x} = \$540, \ \sigma_x = \$106$
options.why: Added the $\$45$ to the standard deviation instead of the mean, swapping which statistic a constant shift affects.

questions.solution_text:
$\overline{x} = 540 + 45 = \$585$
Every wage shifts by the same amount, so the spread — and therefore $\sigma_x = \$61$ — is unchanged.

questions.question_text:
A gym class has a mean of $30$ push-ups and population standard deviation $4$ push-ups.
Every member's count is then reduced by $6$ push-ups after a stricter counting rule.
What are the new mean and standard deviation?

options.text: $\overline{x} = 30, \ \sigma_x = 10$
options.why: Applied the $6$ to the standard deviation instead of the mean, and added it rather than recognising the spread is unaffected.

options.text: $\overline{x} = 24, \ \sigma_x = 10$
options.why: Reduced the mean correctly but also changed the standard deviation, adding the $6$ to it as though the class became more spread out.

options.text: $\overline{x} = 24, \ \sigma_x = 4$
$\overline{x} = 30, \ \sigma_x = 4$
options.why: Assumed a stricter counting rule affects neither statistic, so the reduction was never applied to the mean.

questions.solution_text:
$\overline{x} = 30 - 6 = 24$
Every count shifts down by the same amount, so the spread — and therefore $\sigma_x = 4$ — is unchanged.

questions.question_text:
Six employees have wages with mean $\$720$ and population standard deviation $\$55$.
A new employee joins earning exactly $\$720$.
What happens to the standard deviation?

options.text: It decreases, because the new wage is exactly at the mean and pulls the average distance down.
It increases, because adding any new value increases the spread of the data.
options.why: Assumed any new value must increase the spread, ignoring where it sits relative to the mean.

options.text: It stays exactly the same, because adding one value to six barely changes anything.
options.why: Ignored that a value equal to the mean genuinely reduces the average distance from it.

options.text: It cannot be determined without recalculating from the full dataset.
options.why: Overlooked that a value at the mean reliably decreases the standard deviation.

questions.solution_text:
The new wage, $\$720$, has a distance of $\$0$ from the mean, which is less than the current standard deviation of $\$55$.
Including it pulls the average distance from the mean down, so $\sigma_x$ decreases.

questions.question_text:
Five gym members have a mean of $18$ push-ups and population standard deviation $2.5$ push-ups.
A new member joins and manages $50$ push-ups.
What happens to the standard deviation?

options.text: It increases, because the new value is far above the mean and pulls the average distance up.
It decreases, because a very high score balances out the lower scores in the group.
options.why: Confused balancing the mean with reducing the spread.

options.text: It stays the same, because standard deviation only changes when every value changes.
options.why: Overlooked that a single extreme new value changes the spread.

options.text: It increases only if the new member's score is added twice.
options.why: Introduced an irrelevant condition not implied by adding one new value.

questions.solution_text:
The new value, $50$, is $32$ push-ups from the mean of $18$ — far more than the current standard deviation of $2.5$ push-ups.
Including it pulls the average distance from the mean up, so $\sigma_x$ increases.

questions.question_text:
A café currently pays $5$ casual staff different hourly rates, with population standard deviation $\$3.20$.
The owner proposes paying every staff member exactly the same rate, equal to the current mean rate.
What will the new standard deviation be?

options.text: It becomes $0$, because there is no spread when every value is identical.
It stays $\$3.20$, because the spread between the staff has not changed.
options.why: Failed to recognise that making every value identical removes all spread.

options.text: It cannot be exactly $0$, because a standard deviation is never zero.
options.why: Assumed a standard deviation can never be exactly zero, even for identical values.

options.text: It becomes equal to the mean rate, because standard deviation equals the mean for uniform data.
options.why: Confused the standard deviation with the mean for a uniform dataset.

questions.solution_text:
$\sigma_x = 0$
When every staff member is paid the same rate, there is no spread at all between the wages.

questions.question_text:
A fitness class's push-up results have mean $26$ and $\sigma_x = 4.1$.
Which of the following changes would leave $\sigma_x$ unchanged?
(i) Every member does $5$ more push-ups.
(ii) A new member joins doing $26$ push-ups.
(iii) A new member joins doing $60$ push-ups.

options.text: Only (i), because a uniform shift doesn't change the spread, while the new members in (ii) and (iii) do.
(i) and (ii), because a value at the mean doesn't add any spread.
options.why: Assumed a value exactly at the mean has zero effect, when it actually decreases the standard deviation.

options.text: All three, because none of these changes affects the individual push-up counts already in the dataset.
options.why: Overlooked that adding a new value changes the dataset even without altering the existing counts.

options.text: None of them, because standard deviation always changes whenever anything about the dataset changes.
options.why: Assumed every change to a dataset must alter the standard deviation.

questions.solution_text:
(i) A uniform shift leaves the spread — and $\sigma_x$ — unchanged.
(ii) A value at the mean pulls the average distance down, so $\sigma_x$ decreases.
(iii) A value far above the mean increases the spread, so $\sigma_x$ increases.
Only (i) leaves $\sigma_x$ unchanged.

questions.question_text:
A team of $5$ employees has a mean wage of $\$800$ and population standard deviation $\$60$.
Every employee receives a $\$150$ pay rise.
What are the new mean and standard deviation?

options.text: The mean is $\$950$ and the standard deviation is $\$60$.
The mean is $\$950$ and the standard deviation is $\$210$.
options.why: Added the $\$150$ rise to the standard deviation as well as to the mean, although a uniform shift leaves the spread unchanged.

options.text: The mean is $\$800$ and the standard deviation is $\$60$.
options.why: Recognised that the spread is unchanged but failed to increase the mean by $\$150$.

options.text: The mean is $\$830$ and the standard deviation is $\$60$.
options.why: Divided the $\$150$ rise by the $5$ employees, although each employee receives the full rise.

questions.solution_text:
The new mean is $800+150=\$950$.
Every wage increases by the same $\$150$, so the spread is unchanged.
The population standard deviation remains $\$60$.

questions.question_text: A dataset of $5$ values has population standard deviation $15$. Each value is increased by $2$. What is the new standard deviation?

options.why: Divided the standard deviation $15$ by the number of values, $5$. A constant shift does not change the spread.
Calculated $15\times5+2$, treating the number of values and the shift as changes to the standard deviation.
Calculated $(15-2)\div5$. The $2$ is added to each data value, not subtracted from the standard deviation, and the spread is unchanged.

questions.solution_text:
Every value increases by the same $2$, so the whole dataset shifts without changing its spread.
The mean increases by $2$, but the population standard deviation stays $15$.
